prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Health Interview Survey
 

About NHIS

For Everyone
June 18, 2026

What to know

  • NHIS is the National Health Interview Survey.
  • NHIS is a national survey that monitors the health of the U.S. population.
  • NHIS statistics provide insights into the health of people of different ages, sexes, races and ethnicities, geographic locations, and social and economic circumstances.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics. NHIS focuses on the health of U.S. children and adults.

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) conducts NHIS. It is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey. NHIS began collecting data in 1957.

Each year, NHIS collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews throughout the year. Many of these adults also provide health information about children in their households.

NHIS collects data from civilians who don't live in institutions. Civilians are people not serving on active duty in the military. Institutionalized people live in places like correctional facilities, skilled-nursing homes, and mental (psychiatric) hospitals.

NCHS is exploring new ways for you to participate in NHIS. Some people may receive a paper questionnaire while others will receive an invitation to complete the survey online. Some people may receive both. Your participation matters no matter how you complete the survey. If you need assistance with the survey or have questions, please call the number on the letter you received or email nhis@census.gov.

Selected to participate in the survey?

Learn why you should take part in NHIS and what to expect.
Visit our participant website

What's collected

NHIS collects data through personal interviews. One adult household member provides information about their own health and the health of others in their households.

NHIS collects data about health topics like—

  • Illness and chronic conditions
  • Injuries and chronic pain
  • Health-related behaviors
  • Ability to perform daily activities (functioning) and disability
  • Healthcare access and use
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Preventive services to identify and prevent health problems

The U.S. Census Bureau employs and trains field staff to conduct these interviews. They follow procedures developed by NCHS experts. Field staff conduct most interviews in person. Sometimes they conduct follow-up interviews over the phone.

Did you know?

NHIS content is updated about every 15–20 years to reflect advances in survey methodology and coverage of health topics. In 2019, NHIS launched redesigned content and structure that differs from the earlier questionnaire design (1997–2018).

Data and documentation

NCHS publishes reports featuring expert analysis of NHIS data. Selected estimates also are available as part of our interactive data query systems that provide tables and charts.

In producing these resources, NHIS staff prioritize protecting participants' privacy.

Data files

NHIS public use data files are available to download in multiple formats. All potentially identifiable information has been removed to ensure the confidentiality of participants and their households.

NHIS restricted data files are available through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center (RDC) for a fee. To access restricted NHIS data, researchers must submit requests in the Standard Application Process portal. The RDC provides instructions for preparing and submitting an application to access restricted data.

NHIS data also has been linked with data from other sources. This provides more robust datasets that can be used to analyze complex relationships between data from different sources. These linked datasets are available in the RDC.

Find data documentation for these datasets at Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation.

How the data are used

NCHS staff use NHIS data to produce official national health estimates. One of NHIS's key strengths is its ability to produce estimates for many subgroups of the U.S. population. NHIS can do this because it collects data from such a large group of people.

NHIS health statistics provide health information by—

  • Demographic characteristics, like age and marital status
  • Geographic location, like region and metro area size
  • Social and economic circumstances, like employment status and poverty level

These data help researchers, policymakers, and other data users better understand how health differs among these groups.

NHIS data drive policies and programs to improve health. NHIS results have helped track the health status of Americans, their access to health care, and the nation's progress toward achieving health goals.

Email nhis@cdc.gov with any questions about the National Health Interview Survey.

Resources on this page provide information about the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) data collection, its participants, and its protocols. It also provides analytic notes and references. They will help you understand, analyze, and use NHIS data.

Data linked to NHIS data

Linking data is combining two or more datasets that have some related variables to create a new dataset. The new linked dataset maximizes the value of the original data. Researchers can analyze the new linked dataset to understand the relationships between different variables using data collected separately. For example, linking NHCS data with data from the National Death Index (NDI) produces a dataset that can be used to measure mortality after a patient left the hospital. These linked data also can provide information about the patient's cause of death.

NHIS data has been linked with data from several other sources, including NDI, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Access to these linked datasets is restricted and provided through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center.

Other NHIS survey data

NHIS-Teen

NHIS-Teen is a web-based survey of young people ages 12–17 years whose parent participated in NHIS on their behalf. NHIS-Teen provides data about teens from teens.

Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

In 2014, NHIS conducted the Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS (NHPI NHIS). This survey collected information about the health of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders in all 50 states.

Find data and related resources from that survey on the NPHI NHIS questionnaires, datasets, and documentation page.

National Immunization Provider Record Check Study

NCHS and CDC's National Immunization Program implemented the NHIS/National Immunization Provider Record Check Study (NHIS/NIPRCS) in 1994 to determine the accuracy of the household vaccination reports for children aged 12–35 months.

NIPRCS's was to validate the children’s vaccination histories reported in the NHIS Immunization Supplement against the records obtained from the immunization providers for these children.

Find data and related resources from that survey in the CDC Archive.

2028 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign

For Everyone
Aug. 21, 2026

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is proposing updates to the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).
  • NCHS is redesigning NHIS to modernize its data collection process.
  • The redesign is in response to rising costs, growing difficulty in reaching households, and the need for a more flexible and efficient survey.

Overview

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has proposed a redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Since 1957, NHIS has collected and analyzed health data to monitor the health of people across the country.

The proposed NHIS redesign includes—

  • Revisions to the adult and child questionnaires
  • Use of a sequential mixed-mode data collection design with self-response options

Changes to the questionnaires are intended to improve the measurement of contemporary health topics and reduce respondent burden through shorter and less complex instruments.

The redesign reflects the ongoing need to maintain a gold-standard national health survey while adapting to increasing data collection costs and respondent preferences by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered data collection modes.

NHIS was previously redesigned in 1997 and 2019.

Proposed content

Review the draft questionnaires and a brief description of the redesign (in the Federal Register) to learn more—

  • Adult Questionnaire
  • Child Questionnaire
  • Federal Register Notice

Public comment

NCHS invites public comment on all areas of the proposed redesign. Comments are especially welcome regarding—

  • Structure, length, and clarity of the revised questionnaire
  • Shift to a sequential mixed mode design
  • Proposed addition or removal of content
  • How these changes may affect data quality, usability, and trends over time

Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified data needs.

NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., population estimates that have historically relied on data from both the adult and child-focused interviews).

Questions?

Email healthsurveys@cdc.gov with any questions about the 2028 redesign.

Comment submission

Written comments must be received on or before October 20, 2026.

You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 by any of the following methods:

  • Federal eRulemaking Portal:
    • Go to the Federal Register Notice
    • Click on the blue "Comment" button at the top to submit comments
  • Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road, N.E., MS-D74, Atlanta, Georgia 30329

By Julia A. Rivera Drew

Collected annually since 1957, the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is the longest running nationally-representative health survey in the world. The NHIS questionnaire and data collection approaches have changed considerably over time, both to better capture emerging public health topics as well as to adapt the study design, questionnaire, and data collection operations to maintain a high-quality data product. The objective of this blog post is understanding the factors that contribute to year-to-year change in variables available from the NHIS with a particular focus on the 2025 NHIS data.

How is the NHIS structured?

Since 2019, the NHIS questionnaire has been a combination of (1) NHIS “core” content, collected every year; (2) NHIS “rotating core” content, collected on some predetermined occasional schedule; (3) NHIS “emerging public health” topical content, which is generally temporary and may be collected for a few consecutive years, collected occasionally, or collected once and then not again; and (4) NHIS “sponsored” content, with funding provided by other federal agencies. Refer to our user note on changes to the NHIS questionnaire implemented with the 2019 redesign for more information.

Why might specific variables be discontinued?

Changes to NHIS variables from one year to the next are by and large expected and due to intentional design choices or priorities of the question sponsors. One such intentional design choice is the implementation of rotating core content with the 2019 NHIS redesign. For example, a set of items on utilization of health care services such as dental, vision, and home health care is asked on a two-years-on-one-year-off rotation (e.g., DENTINT, “interval since last dental visit,” was collected in 2019-2020, skipped in 2021, collected in 2022-2023, skipped in 2024, and collection resumed in 2025). When a major change to NHIS core content is proposed, users are formally notified through a federal register notice (such as the recent federal notice about proposed changes to the NHIS questionnaire to be implemented in 2028).

The discontinuation of emerging public health and sponsored content is harder to predict. For example, the 2019 and 2020 questionnaires included three items of emerging public health content on using opioid use for pain, which quickly gave way in 2021 to a series of COVID-19 related measures designed to track important public health aspects of the pandemic, such as testing, infection, vaccination, social distancing, and social isolation. Sustaining sponsored content, where open-ended supplements are fielded on an annual or otherwise regular basis, is clearly distinguished from other, close-ended sponsored content in the NHIS documentation. However, even sustaining sponsors can reduce or completely end their support for long-running questions on the NHIS questionnaire with little notice, as was the case for the food security supplement items that have been sponsored by USDA for inclusion in the NHIS since 2011. The discontinuation of these items was disclosed at the beginning of 2025 and described in greater detail below.

IPUMS integrates new NHIS data into our collection and makes them available through the nhis.ipums.org website as quickly as possible. However, we frequently break the release of new NHIS data to the IPUMS NHIS website into two parts, adding continuing content first and new or modified content later. If we have not added a variable of interest to you, please consult the original NCHS documentation before concluding that it is no longer available.

Which NHIS variables have been discontinued with the release of 2025 data?

In our initial data processing of the 2025 NHIS sample, released at the end of August 2026, we observed that multiple long-standing items were absent. Below, we describe the long-standing items that we noticed were absent as of this writing.

Food Security

Notably, there were no food security items included with the 2025 data, including an additional measure on SNAP benefit receipt in the past 30 days. The absence of these measures was an expected discontinuation, documented in an updated footnote in NCHS documentation about NHIS sustaining sponsors, as described in this IPUMS blog post about the broader discontinuation of USDA-sponsored food security items on household surveys.

Immunization

Multiple items from an immunization supplement sponsored by the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases (NCIRD) were also absent from the 2025 data (refer to Table 1 below), although NCIRD is still identified as a sustaining NHIS sponsor and sponsored several continuing immunization measures. The discontinuation of some immunization measures could simply reflect the removal of items that have declined in importance with shifts in the landscape of vaccination practice, such as questions about the number of COVID-19 vaccine doses or brand of COVID-19 vaccine first received. Measures of ever having received a COVID-19 vaccination continue. Similarly, we observed removal of items asking about a specific brand name of shingles vaccine (Zostavax) but the retention of an “ever received” shingles vaccine variable.

A handful of other items continue to be of substantial public health importance (Callahan et al. 2021; Cambou et al. 2021; Meghani et al. 2023; Evensen-Martinez et al. 2026; Gibson and Greene 2020, Guardiano et al. 2024; Srinivasan, et al. 2021; Sulley et al. 2025) and their exclusion from the 2025 data was unexpected. Five long-running immunization items – three items about flu shots during pregnancy – PREGFLUYR_A (IPUMS NHIS variable PREGFLUYR), FLUSHPG1 (PREGFLUSH), and FLUSHPG2 (PREGFLUSH) – and two items about whether sample adults worked or volunteered in a health care setting – WRKHLTH (WORKVOLHCSET) and WRKDIR (WORKVOLHCPAT and WORKVOLMED) – were not included in the 2025 data.

The immunization items that were absent from the 2025 questionnaire are not part of NHIS “core” content, meaning that they are not paid for by NCHS. Instead, they are part of an immunization supplement sponsored by NCIRD. We would expect questionnaire content to change from year-to-year to better meet public health surveillance needs. NHIS questionnaire content may also change from year-to-year because of real funding constraints and shifting sponsor priorities. The rationale for the modification or removal of content is not always clear. And it is, of course, always possible that these measures will reappear on the questionnaire in the future.

Newly Announced Proposed Changes to the NHIS Questionnaire

On August 20, 2026, NCHS published a Federal Register notice asking for public comment on proposed changes to the NHIS questionnaire – the deadline for comment is October 20. Note that the proposed changes to the NHIS questionnaire described in the Federal Register notice are distinct from the changes to the 2025 NHIS content discussed above. IPUMS NHIS is reviewing and summarizing the proposed changes and highlighting helpful resources for responding to the Federal Register notice; we will update our summary document with additional information from other organizations, data users, and our own assessments. Note that the IPUMS NHIS website provides information at a glance on the availability of specific measures, organized by topic, and makes it easy to examine changes in question phrasing over time.

NHIS Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation

At a glance

  • Explore this gateway to data from the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).
  • Find survey methods, questionnaires, and other resources to collect NHIS data.
  • Access important technical information to help you understand, analyze, and use NHIS data.

Overview

Resources on this page provide information about the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) data collection, its participants, and its protocols. It also provides analytic notes and references. They will help you understand, analyze, and use NHIS data.

Find survey instruments, data, and other resources by year at—

  • 2026 NHIS Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation
  • 2025 NHIS Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation

Resources from earlier survey years are available through the CDC Archive. There you will find older NHIS questionnaires, datasets, and documentation.

  • 1996 and earlier

Data linked to NHIS data

Linking data is combining two or more datasets that have some related variables to create a new dataset. The new linked dataset maximizes the value of the original data. Researchers can analyze the new linked dataset to understand the relationships between different variables using data collected separately. For example, linking NHCS data with data from the National Death Index (NDI) produces a dataset that can be used to measure mortality after a patient left the hospital. These linked data also can provide information about the patient's cause of death.

NHIS data has been linked with data from several other sources, including NDI, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Access to these linked datasets is restricted and provided through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center.

Other NHIS survey data

NHIS-Teen

NHIS-Teen is a web-based survey of young people ages 12–17 years whose parent participated in NHIS on their behalf. NHIS-Teen provides data about teens from teens.

Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

In 2014, NHIS conducted the Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS (NHPI NHIS). This survey collected information about the health of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders in all 50 states.

Find data and related resources from that survey on the NPHI NHIS questionnaires, datasets, and documentation page.

National Immunization Provider Record Check Study

NCHS and CDC's National Immunization Program implemented the NHIS/National Immunization Provider Record Check Study (NHIS/NIPRCS) in 1994 to determine the accuracy of the household vaccination reports for children aged 12–35 months.

NIPRCS's was to validate the children’s vaccination histories reported in the NHIS Immunization Supplement against the records obtained from the immunization providers for these children.

Find data and related resources from that survey in the CDC Archive.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Health Interview Survey: research and preservation report

**Research checked:** October 8, 2026  
**Official publisher:** National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)  
**Official website:** https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

## Executive assessment

The **National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)** is a foundational federal statistical program measuring health, disability, health insurance, healthcare access, and related characteristics of the U.S. **civilian noninstitutionalized population**. It began interviewing in **July 1957**.

NHIS is better understood as a **continuing survey and a collection of annual datasets, questionnaires, documentation, statistical reports, and linked-data products**, rather than one unchanging dataset.

Its principal strengths are:

- A long historical record of population health.
- Nationally representative probability sampling.
- Health information about people regardless of whether they have insurance or receive medical care.
- The ability to examine differences by demographic and socioeconomic characteristics.
- Free public-use microdata, complemented by controlled access to more detailed information.
- Its role in supporting other surveys and linked administrative-data research.

Its main limitations are:

- Important exclusions from the population covered.
- Self-reported and proxy-reported information rather than clinical examinations.
- Nonresponse and declining response rates.
- Changes in questionnaire content, sampling, and interview mode.
- Limited public-use geographic detail.
- Disruptions that complicate interpretation of particular years.

**Preservation priority: high.** Neither historical interviews nor the surrounding methodological context can simply be recreated later.

---

## 1. Verification of the information you supplied

| Supplied information | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Title: National Health Interview Survey** | Correct. Common abbreviation: **NHIS**. |
| **Publisher: CDC, NCHS** | Correct. More fully: **HHS → CDC → NCHS**. The Census Bureau is a major operational partner, not the primary statistical publisher. |
| **Monitors adult and child health through a broad range of topics** | Correct. |
| **Collecting data since 1957** | Correct; interviewing began in **July 1957**. |
| **Nation’s largest and oldest national health survey** | This reproduces CDC’s own description. For cataloging, “long-running national household health interview survey” is more precise than an unqualified superlative, which depends on the surveys being compared. |
| **About 27,000 adults each year** | A reasonable general description retained on CDC’s overview page, but **not a fixed annual count**. Actual sample sizes vary. The 2025 design aimed for approximately **30,000 adult interviews**; 2025 ultimately included **24,215**. |
| **Confidential, face-to-face interviews** | Confidentiality is correct. “Face-to-face” is incomplete: telephone interviewing is substantial, pandemic procedures differed, and self-administered modes are being tested and proposed for a future redesign. |
| **URL** | Correct and functioning when checked. |

For example, in **2025**, **53.1% of adult interviews and 54.3% of child interviews were conducted at least partly by telephone**. Thus, the supplied description is broadly accurate but understates current methodological complexity.

**Sources:** [CDC overview](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/index.html); [2025 survey description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/srvydesc-508.pdf).

### Suggested replacement catalog description

> The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is a continuing, nationally representative household survey conducted by CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics, with data collection carried out by the U.S. Census Bureau. Initiated in July 1957, it measures health status, disability, health behaviors, health insurance, and healthcare access and use among the U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized population. Annual public-use datasets contain information about sampled adults and children, with sample sizes and content varying by year. Data are collected through confidential interviews, using in-person and telephone methods, with additional modes being tested and proposed.

---

## 2. Publisher, institutional responsibilities, and governance

### NCHS: statistical owner and publisher

NCHS is responsible for the survey’s statistical purpose, questionnaire development, methodological specifications, data processing and analysis, confidentiality protections, documentation, and dissemination.

The program is associated with NCHS’s **Division of Health Interview Statistics**.

### Census Bureau: collection and sampling partner

Under an interagency arrangement, the **U.S. Census Bureau** participates in sampling and field operations. It employs and trains field representatives who conduct interviews following NCHS procedures.

This distinction matters for provenance:

- **Publisher/statistical authority:** NCHS.
- **Parent agencies:** CDC and HHS.
- **Collection partner:** Census Bureau.
- **Secondary distributor or harmonizer:** for example, IPUMS—not the original collector.

### Other agencies and sponsors

Federal agencies can fund additional questionnaire content. Sponsored modules allow NHIS to address particular policy and research needs, but their availability depends on the year and sponsorship.

NHIS also provides the responding-household sampling frame for AHRQ’s **Medical Expenditure Panel Survey Household Component (MEPS-HC)**.

**Sources:** [CDC overview](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/index.html); [sample-design report](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/series/sr_02/sr02-191.pdf); [2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

---

## 3. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### Original authority

The **National Health Survey Act of 1956**, Public Law **84-652**, enacted **July 3, 1956**, called for a continuing survey and special studies concerning the amount, distribution, and effects of illness and disability, and associated services.

NHIS began the following year.

### Current statistical mandate

The principal authority is **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act**, codified at **42 U.S.C. § 242k**.

Especially important is **§ 242k(h)(2)**:

> “There shall be an annual collection of data from a statistically valid sample concerning the general health, illness, and disability status of the civilian noninstitutionalized population.”

The provision specifies annual or periodic coverage of injuries, chronic diseases and impairments, disability, physician visits, hospitalizations, and relationships between demographic, socioeconomic, and health characteristics.

**Interpretation:** The statutory obligation is stronger than merely authorizing an optional survey. However, the law does not freeze the NHIS questionnaire, sample size, or collection mode in its present form.

### Administrative clearance

NHIS uses **OMB control number 0920-0214**. Paperwork Reduction Act clearance creates a separate mechanism for reviewing instruments, respondent burden, and proposed changes. Federal Register notices offer opportunities for public comment.

The obligation to conduct the statistical program is distinct from participation by an individual household: **NHIS participation is voluntary**.

### Confidentiality authority

Major protections include:

- **Public Health Service Act § 308(d), 42 U.S.C. § 242m(d)**.
- **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act of 2018 (CIPSEA), 44 U.S.C. §§ 3561–3583**.
- The **Privacy Act of 1974**, as described in survey documentation.

Identifiable responses cannot simply be repurposed for administrative or enforcement uses. CDC states that willful unauthorized disclosure by covered personnel can result in **up to five years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to $250,000, or both**.

Public-use files are therefore not releases of unrestricted original interview records.

**Sources:** [Current U.S. Code](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title42-section242k); [NCHS legislative history](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/misc/legislation2014.pdf); [participant confidentiality statement](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis-participants/about/privacy.html); [Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

---

## 4. History and major discontinuities

| Period | Significance |
|---|---|
| **1956** | National Health Survey Act enacted. |
| **July 1957** | Survey interviewing begins. |
| **1960** | NCHS established through the merger of the National Health Survey and the federal vital-statistics organization. |
| **1963 onward** | Public-use digital microdata are available. This is not the same as the survey’s 1957 starting date. |
| **1963–1967** | Historical files use fiscal-year reporting periods. |
| **1968** | Transition from fiscal-year to calendar-year reporting; some corresponding files overlap. Questionnaire approaches also changed during the transition. |
| **1997–2018** | A major questionnaire era with household/family/person information and Sample Adult and Sample Child components. |
| **2019** | Major redesign of questionnaire structure and content, reducing burden and organizing annual, rotating, sponsored, and emerging content. |
| **2020** | COVID-19 disrupted collection modes and introduced a special reinterviewed adult component. |
| **2025** | New sample design based on the 2020 Census, annual selection of housing units, and major operational disruptions. |
| **2028, proposed** | Shorter questionnaires and sequential mixed-mode collection, including online and paper self-response followed by some in-person follow-up. |

### Preservation implications of early files

NCHS’s availability summary states that **no data files are available before 1963**. That does not mean there are no earlier publications or questionnaires worth preserving.

Historical release dates can be much later than interview dates. For example, the **1968 public-use release README is dated March 24, 2008**, and says the files had not previously been distributed.

Catalogs should therefore distinguish:

1. Interview/reference period.
2. Survey-year label.
3. Original publication date.
4. Microdata release date.
5. Revision date.
6. Repository accession date.

**Sources:** [Data availability summary](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Datasets/NHIS/summary.pdf); [1963 README](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/1963/readme.txt); [1968 README](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/1968/readme.txt); [documentation gateway](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/index.html).

---

## 5. Population, coverage, and collection methods

### Who is represented?

The target is the **civilian noninstitutionalized population residing in the 50 states and Washington, DC**.

Important exclusions identified in recent documentation include:

- Active-duty military personnel.
- Civilians living on military bases.
- People in long-term-care and correctional institutions.
- People with no fixed household address.

U.S. territories are outside the stated 50-state-and-DC target.

**Consequently, “the U.S. population” should not be interpreted as every U.S. resident.** Exclusions are particularly consequential for disability, aging, incarceration, and homelessness research.

### Sampling and respondents

Recent NHIS designs select:

- **One adult aged 18 or older** from each sampled household.
- **One child under 18**, where children are present.

Adults normally report for themselves. A knowledgeable proxy can respond when the selected adult is physically or cognitively unable to do so.

Child information comes from an adult knowledgeable about and responsible for the child’s healthcare—not generally from the child directly.

### Survey type

NHIS is principally a **repeated cross-sectional survey**. It measures changing populations over time rather than routinely following the same people each year.

Special follow-ups, administrative linkages, and reinterview projects can support longitudinal research, but they do not make the ordinary annual NHIS a conventional panel survey.

### Collection

Recent annual documentation describes **computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI)**, generally initiated in homes, supplemented by telephone interviews.

English and Spanish questionnaires, instrument flowcharts, advance letters, and field manuals are available. These documents are valuable evidence of how the data were actually produced.

**Sources:** [2025 reporting checklist](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/2025-NHIS-PRICSSA-508.pdf); [2025 materials](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/2025-nhis.html).

## 6. What the data contain

NHIS covers a wide range of topics, including:

- General health and diagnosed chronic conditions.
- Disability and functional limitations.
- Injuries and chronic pain.
- Mental health and related measures, where included.
- Health insurance.
- Healthcare access, delays, unmet need, and use.
- Preventive services and screening.
- Tobacco, alcohol, physical activity, sleep, and other behaviors.
- Child health and development-related topics.
- Demographic, employment, educational, household, and income characteristics.

**Not every topic or measure appears every year.**

Since 2019, the questionnaire has distinguished:

1. **Annual core:** fielded every year.
2. **Rotating core:** scheduled periodically.
3. **Sponsored content:** supported by other agencies.
4. **Emerging content:** new topics supported by NCHS.

For scientific reuse, the essential unit of documentation is **variable × survey year × eligible population × exact wording × collection conditions**.

A matching variable name does not by itself establish comparability.

## 9. Essential analytical guidance for data scientists

### Survey weights and design variables are indispensable

For recent public-use files, the standard variables include:

| Purpose | Adult | Child |
|---|---|---|
| Final person weight | `WTFA_A` | `WTFA_C` |
| Public-use stratum | `PSTRAT` | `PSTRAT` |
| Public-use primary sampling unit | `PPSU` | `PPSU` |

NCHS identifies **Taylor-series linearization** for variance estimation.

An ordinary unweighted mean or regression may describe the responding sample but should not automatically be presented as a national estimate. Ignoring clustering and stratification can also produce misleading standard errors.

### Other critical precautions

- **Use the correct universe.** Skip patterns, age restrictions, and content eligibility define denominators.
- **Separate missingness types.** Refused, unknown, not ascertained, and not applicable are not interchangeable.
- **Check the codebook before recoding numeric values.**
- **Use multiple-imputation methods** for imputed income, including uncertainty across imputations.
- **Use pair weights** for analyses targeting parent–child pairs; ordinary adult or child weights may be inappropriate.
- **Follow pooling instructions.** Multi-year weights and variance specifications depend on the estimand, years, and special samples.
- **Check redesign boundaries.** The 2019 change is a particularly important break.
- **Distinguish public and restricted design guidance.** NCHS says public-use pooling across the 2025 sampling redesign does not require special adjustment for the redesign in variance estimation; restricted-design users must distinguish strata across designs.
- **Assess subgroup reliability.** Large overall samples do not guarantee precise estimates for rare conditions or small populations.
- **Report uncertainty, not just percentages.**
- **Treat causal claims cautiously.** Cross-sectional associations alone do not establish policy effects.

### Machine-learning considerations

NHIS can support predictive and methodological research, but:

- Models trained on respondents may not generalize to excluded populations.
- Random train/test splits can overlook year, household, and survey-design structure.
- Weighted population performance may differ from unweighted accuracy.
- Coding changes can create artificial predictive signals.
- Identifying individuals or enriching records for identification is outside legitimate statistical reuse.

These are analytical recommendations, not additional official NHIS requirements.

**Source:** [2025 PRICSSA checklist](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/health_statistics/nchs/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2025/2025-NHIS-PRICSSA-508.pdf).

## 10. Linkages, derived resources, and related surveys

### Mortality linkage

NHIS records have been linked to the **National Death Index**, supporting studies of relationships between baseline health and later mortality.

As documented in March 2026:

- Updated restricted files cover NHIS **1986–2021**, with mortality follow-up through **December 31, 2022**.
- Public-use files from an earlier linkage cover NHIS **1986–2018** and contain limited adult mortality information.
- Some public-use follow-up times and causes of death have synthetic substitutions for disclosure protection; vital status was not changed.

**Do not confuse the survey year with the mortality follow-up endpoint.**

### Administrative linkages

NHIS-related resources include links to Medicare, Medicaid/CHIP, HUD housing assistance, and historical Social Security benefit information. Coverage and access differ by linkage.

Linkage eligibility, consent, matching success, and selection must be considered; not every interviewed person has a usable linked record.

### MEPS

NHIS supplies the sampling frame for MEPS-HC. Linkage files connect some MEPS respondents to their previous NHIS responses.

For linked analyses, CDC specifies **MEPS weights and design variables**, with adjustment for unmatched people as appropriate. After the 2019 redesign, public-use NHIS information is available for selected adults and children, not every household member.

### IPUMS Health Surveys

**IPUMS NHIS** harmonizes annual microdata from **1963 onward**, supports custom extracts, and supplies extensive comparability notes.

It is a valuable secondary access route, but harmonization cannot eliminate substantive changes in underlying measurement. Preserve the exact extract, harmonized metadata, and version.

### Related collections

- **NHIS-Teen:** web-based self-reports from adolescents aged 12–17 whose parent participated on their behalf.
- **2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS:** a special population-focused survey.
- **NHIS/National Immunization Provider Record Check Study:** validation of household vaccination reports against provider records.

These require their own sampling and analytic documentation and should not be casually appended to ordinary annual NHIS files.

## 11. Typical users and benefits to the public

| User community | Typical uses |
|---|---|
| **NCHS, CDC, and HHS analysts** | Official prevalence estimates, health surveillance, national objectives, and program monitoring. |
| **Epidemiologists and academic researchers** | Chronic disease, disability, mental health, health behavior, disparities, and mortality research. |
| **Health economists and policy researchers** | Insurance coverage, access barriers, utilization, and relationships between socioeconomic circumstances and health. |
| **Government and legislative analysts** | Evidence for policy debate, program design, and evaluation. |
| **Public health practitioners and nonprofits** | Identifying broad unmet needs and populations experiencing disadvantage. |
| **Journalists and advocates** | Public communication and independent scrutiny of national health claims. |
| **Data librarians and educators** | Data discovery, methods instruction, reproducible research, and historical documentation. |

### Public benefits

**1. Measures needs that medical records miss.**  
Unlike claims or electronic health records alone, NHIS can capture uninsured people, people who have not recently received care, and reported unmet needs.

**2. Supports public accountability.**  
It supplies evidence against which claims about coverage, prevention, disability, and healthcare access can be assessed.

**3. Makes disparities measurable.**  
Its demographic and socioeconomic information supports examination of differences across groups.

**4. Preserves historical perspective.**  
Long-term records show how health burdens and healthcare circumstances change—provided methodological breaks are respected.

**5. Provides a reusable public research resource.**  
Free microdata allow independent analyses beyond the original agency’s publications.

**6. Supports statistical infrastructure.**  
NHIS supports MEPS and is used to benchmark and calibrate other survey products, including NCHS rapid surveys.

**7. Increases value through linkage.**  
Administrative and mortality links allow questions that interviews alone cannot answer without conducting an entirely new survey.

These are benefits and mechanisms, not a quantified estimate of lives saved or financial return attributable to NHIS.

## 12. Preservation plan for an archive or data library

### Minimum complete preservation package

For each year, preserve:

1. Original compressed data files.
2. Extracted data files.
3. Adult, child, and other applicable components.
4. Codebooks and variable summaries.
5. Exact questionnaires, including language versions.
6. Survey descriptions and analytic guidance.
7. Input programs and format definitions.
8. Income imputations and their documentation.
9. Special weights, pair files, and linkage instructions.
10. Field manuals, flowcharts, and participant materials.
11. Paradata documentation and files, where released.
12. Checksum lists, README files, errata, and revision notices.
13. Relevant official tables and reports.
14. Captured landing pages and source-link relationships.
15. OMB and Federal Register documentation for major changes.

### Preservation practices

- Retain **bit-for-bit originals**; store normalized versions separately.
- Generate SHA-256 checksums and compare official checksums where supplied.
- Record download dates, exact URLs, file sizes, and revision labels.
- Validate row counts and variable counts against official summaries.
- Preserve numeric codes and labels, not merely displayed text.
- Retain fixed-width layouts and character-encoding information.
- Record all transformations in executable code.
- Maintain multiple geographically separate copies and regular fixity checks.
- Assign repository identifiers to preserved release packages.
- Preserve archived website content as well as current pages.
- Avoid executing historical self-extracting `.EXE` archives; prefer ZIP versions.
- Never mirror restricted identifiable records without appropriate authorization.

### Why documentation is as important as the data

Without universes, weights, questionnaires, and design notes, an archive may preserve readable numbers but lose the ability to interpret them correctly.

The **1968 overlap**, **2019 redesign**, **2020 special sample**, and **2025 collection interruption** are concrete examples of context that must travel with the files.

### Useful catalog fields

Include:

- Survey title and acronym.
- Publisher and collection partner.
- Survey year and actual collection dates.
- Target population and exclusions.
- Unit of observation.
- Component/file name.
- Geographic coverage and available geographic detail.
- Sample size and response-rate definition.
- Collection mode.
- Questionnaire/design era.
- Weight and variance variables.
- Formats and software support.
- Access level and confidentiality terms.
- Release and revision dates.
- Relationships to imputations, pair files, and linkages.
- Persistent identifier, source URL, access date, and checksums.

## 13. Policy watch: proposed 2028 redesign

CDC’s August 2026 proposal would introduce:

- Shorter adult and child instruments.
- Online and paper self-response invitations.
- In-person follow-up for some nonresponding households.
- Revised content and less reliance on a fixed long-term rotating schedule.

The stated reasons include rising collection costs, difficulty reaching households, changing respondent preferences, and the need for flexibility.

**This is proposed—not yet an accomplished change to the annual series.** CDC states that draft questionnaires are expected to be revised after public comment.

### Issues worth scrutinizing

- Which historical measures would disappear?
- Which time series would become discontinuous?
- How would mode effects be assessed?
- Would shorter child content reduce research on child-specific health needs?
- Would online and paper response improve participation equitably?
- What bridging studies and comparability guidance would be released?
- Would smaller or disadvantaged populations retain adequate representation?
- Would public access, documentation, and release timeliness remain strong?

CDC’s redesign page lists **October 20, 2026** as the written-comment deadline. The Federal Register notice should be consulted for submission instructions.

**Sources:** [2028 redesign page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/2028-questionnaire-redesign.html); [Federal Register proposal](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

# NHIS dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 8, 2026**  
**Dataset:** National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)  
**Primary publisher/location:** CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), [NHIS website](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html)

## Overall finding

**The strongest demonstrated risks are loss of particular data elements, interruptions in collection, and institutional capacity—not wholesale disappearance of NHIS.** Annual public-use files continue to be released, historical collections remain linked, and statutory requirements provide substantial protection.

However, additional research uncovered an important qualification to my earlier report: **NCHS says that gender-identity information collected in 2024 is unavailable both in the public-use file and through its Research Data Center, and collection was discontinued in 2025.** Historical accessibility therefore should not be described as entirely unaffected.

These ratings apply your rubric’s categorical triggers; they are **not numerical probabilities of deletion**. I distinguish completed actions from proposals and NHIS/NCHS-specific evidence from broader CDC evidence.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Moderate Risk — supported:** The official **2024 NHIS survey description** identifies gender identity as collected emerging content but states:
  > “These data are not available in the public-use file or through the Research Data Center.”

  It also explicitly connects the collection’s discontinuation in 2025 with Executive Order 14168. This establishes that **an element collected in a prior survey year is unavailable to researchers**, including through the usual restricted-access route.  
  **Source:** [NCHS 2024 survey description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2024/srvydesc-508.pdf).

- **No Known Issue — supported for most historical files, but not the collection as a whole:** CDC’s current gateway still links annual materials for 2019 onward and archived collections for 1997–2018 and earlier years. No evidence located establishes broad removal of entire historical annual files.  
  **Source:** [NHIS documentation gateway](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/index.html).

- **High Risk / Gone — not established:** I did not find evidence that some entire historical annual files have been removed permanently, or that all pre-current-cycle files are unavailable.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

A documented prior-year data element is unavailable. **Important qualification:** the evidence establishes withholding/nonavailability of collected data—not that a previously distributed gender-identity file was subsequently withdrawn. If your rubric requires proof of deletion *from an already released version*, that narrower historical trigger remains unverified.

This finding does not imply that the remaining historical values have been falsified or altered.

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — supported by a partial collection omission:** NCHS’s May 2026 technical notes report that collection paused during the **October 1–November 12, 2025 federal closure**. October and November cases were fielded late, while cases intended for December **“were not fielded in 2025.”** NCHS reports a **1/12 reduction in the annual sample**, with adjusted weights for the missing month.  
  **Source:** [2025 Early Release technical notes](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhis/earlyrelease/earlyrelease202605-tech.pdf).

- **Moderate Risk — also supported:** The same interruption caused collection delays. If “collection skipped” means only cancellation of an *entire annual cycle*, rather than an omitted monthly allocation, Moderate Risk would be the appropriate interpretation.

- **No Known Issue — countervailing evidence:**
  - The **2025 annual public-use files were released in late August 2026** and remain linked.
  - **OMB control number 0920-0214 is active through December 31, 2026**, according to the August 2026 Federal Register notice.
  - NCHS is seeking clearance for continued collection in **2027–2029**, rather than announcing termination.  
  **Sources:** [2025 release page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation/2025-nhis.html); [IPUMS release review](https://blog.popdata.org/continuity-change-in-2025-nhis-data/); [Federal Register notice, August 20, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

- **Gone — not supported:** Neither annual collection nor publication has been terminated. I found no established missed statutory publication deadline or ICR expiration exceeding one year.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Under the rubric’s literal “collection … skipped” trigger, the missing monthly allocation qualifies. **This is a partial collection gap, not a canceled annual survey or evidence that future publication will cease.** Continued publication and active clearance substantially mitigate termination risk.

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — supported by actual reductions in content and analytic detail:**
  - Gender-identity questions were removed from 2025 collection; the collected 2024 information is inaccessible.
  - IPUMS’s September 2026 review identifies missing **food-security and recent SNAP-receipt measures** in the released 2025 data.
  - That review also identifies discontinued immunization-related questions, including **influenza vaccination during pregnancy** and whether respondents work or volunteer in healthcare settings.

  These changes reduce the ability to describe particular populations and study relationships between health, household circumstances, and preventive care.  
  **Sources:** [NCHS 2024 description](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Dataset_Documentation/NHIS/2024/srvydesc-508.pdf); [IPUMS review of 2025 changes](https://blog.popdata.org/continuity-change-in-2025-nhis-data/).

- **Moderate Risk — supported by emerging changes:** The proposed **2028 redesign** would shorten adult and child questionnaires and introduce online and paper self-response before some in-person follow-up. NCHS’s questionnaire-testing justification explicitly anticipates **“substantial cuts”** to survey content. Potential risks include broken time series, mode effects, and reduced child-specific information.  
  **Sources:** [CDC redesign proposal](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/2028-questionnaire-redesign.html); [NCHS testing justification, mirrored OMB submission](https://omb.report/icr/202609-0920-001/doc/172429200.pdf).

- **No Known Issue — mitigating evidence:** NCHS continues to release weights, codebooks, analytic guidance, and other documentation. The proposed mixed-mode approach is intended to improve efficiency and accommodate respondent preferences; it is not inherently evidence of poorer measurement.

- **Gone — not supported:** Collection and publication continue.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Loss of substantive measures has **already occurred**, so this exceeds a merely potential risk. The collection interruption adds uncertainty about seasonal representation and subgroup precision.

**Caution:** NHIS has legitimate rotating and sponsored content. IPUMS explicitly warns that not every disappearing variable represents political interference or deterioration. Some immunization changes may reflect evolving vaccination practice. The High Risk rating concerns demonstrated loss of analytic coverage, not an allegation that all changes were improper or that retained estimates are unreliable.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue — strongly supported:** **42 U.S.C. § 242k(h)(2)** requires:
  > “an annual collection of data from a statistically valid sample concerning the general health, illness, and disability status of the civilian noninstitutionalized population.”

  The provision specifies annual or periodic coverage of injuries, chronic disease and impairment, disability, physician visits, hospitalizations, and relationships between demographic, socioeconomic, and health characteristics.  
  **Source:** [42 U.S.C. § 242k](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title42-section242k).

- **Additional protection through programmatic use:** The 2026 Federal Register notice explicitly coordinates redesign with **Healthy People 2030** monitoring. NHIS also supports research on insurance, access, disability, and federal health programs.  
  **Source:** [Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17040/proposed-data-collection-submitted-for-public-comment-and-recommendations).

- **High / Moderate Risk — not the best fit:** Other surveys measure overlapping topics, but overlap does not eliminate the explicit annual collection requirement or provide a straightforward replacement for NHIS’s full scope and historical series.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

The legal obligation is unusually explicit. Nevertheless, **it protects the statistical function more strongly than every individual variable, exact collection mode, sample size, or existing download URL**. It does not prevent redesign or guarantee unchanged questionnaires.

## Preservation implications

**Preserve NHIS now, but prioritize complete release packages rather than only CSV files.**

1. Save original microdata, codebooks, questionnaires, weights, imputations, checksum lists, and release notices.
2. Preserve 2024–2026 documentation showing content changes and collection interruptions.
3. Capture current and archived landing pages; organizational relocation could change URLs without eliminating underlying files.
4. Monitor renewal of **0920-0214** before its December 2026 expiration and final 2028 redesign decisions.
5. Retain independent copies such as IPUMS extracts, while recognizing that harmonized files are not necessarily bit-for-bit originals.
6. Document unavailable elements explicitly. **Mirroring public files cannot recover data NCHS never released.**

**Research limitation:** This was not a checksum comparison of every historical file. Some official PDFs were accessible to search indexing but could not be fully parsed by the retrieval tool; relevant indexed passages were used. Consequently, broad claims that all historical files are unchanged would be unwarranted.
